newsitem.title: UK: Record UK debt repayment heralds modest tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Record UK debt repayment heralds modest tax cuts.

text.p: British government receipts outstripped expenditure by a massive 4.4 billion pounds in October, official figures released on Monday showed.

The 4.393 billion stg ($7.33 billion) debt repayment over the month, boosted by a flood of corporate tax receipts, was the largest seen in any October since records began in 1968, the Office for National Statistics said.

The figures were a welcome fillip for the government a week before budget day and will make it easier for Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to justify the tax cuts that his Conservative party is baying for with elections due by May 1997.
Clarke said October's public sector debt repayment meant UK public sector debt was well on course to hit his forecast of a 26.9 billion pound shortfall for the 1996/97 year as a whole.
The cumulative public sector borrowing requirement for April to October totalled 11.36 billion pounds. For the same period last year, the shortfall was 18.72 billion.

"These data put the government back on track for its PSBR forecast," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "Although they are unlikely to affect the size of budget tax cuts at this late stage, they do suggest that Clarke will have room to revise down next year's PSBR forecast."
To date, the government is forecasting a public sector borrowing requirement of 23 billion pounds next year.
October traditionally sees a flood of corporate tax receipts pour into the government's coffers but economists had only been expecting an overall debt repayment of about two billion pounds.
As it turned out, corporation tax totalling more than nine billion pounds was collected over the month, compared with little more than seven billion in October last year.
In fact, tax collection was up across the board. About 20 percent more income tax was gathered last month than in October last year and value added tax was also about 20 percent higher.

Most economists expect Clarke to cut taxes to the tune of about three billion pounds in his November 26 budget -- that could mean one penny off the basic rate of income tax, now 24 percent, and a few extra giveaways next year.
Few said Monday's figures would lead to Clarke pushing through larger tax reductions at the last moment. But it will make it easier to justify any tax cuts he does introduce.

"There is no doubt this gives the Chancellor a little bit more room for manoeuvre, though he would prefer a relatively cautious budget this time round if only to minimise the chances of interest rates going up too sharply ahead of the election," said Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International.

Official UK interest rates were raised by a quarter-point to six percent last month. Economists said Clarke may be hard pushed to avoid further rate rises before the election, given that consumer spending is charging ahead and underlying inflation has jumped above three percent.

Economists said the glut of corporation tax in October, although undoubtedly good news for the government, could be offset by a smaller take in January -- the next major month for company tax collection.
"The only question is how much January's corporation tax payment will be reduced correspondingly due to today's figure," said Peter Warburton, economist at Robert Fleming.
Other economists argued that the higher-than-expected haul of not only corporation tax but also value added tax and income tax, suggested the economy is in no need of further stimulus.
"Very strong tax receipts provide additional evidence of the buoyancy of the economy...and hence the lack of need for further stimulus," said BankAmerica economist Jeremy Hawkins.
But with the ruling Conservative Party still trailing in opinion polls and elections only six months away, most expect some attempt to woo back disaffected voters next week.
"We will see some tax cuts. Certainly in gross terms we will see a reduction in the basic rate," said Hannah. ($1=.5994 Stg)
